title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to Europe and the US — go there first so you can get big
dek: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to Europe and the US once they're big, but it's exactly backwards — you go there so you can get big. Pick the wrong region and nothing that follows — product 3.0, the channel pyramid — can be built.
why: Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas-investing experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers; the back half, on AI rebuilding organisations and pricing, has the highest information density.
who: Founders building or preparing to build overseas brands, cross-border e-commerce operators, and early-stage investors watching consumer going-global.
skip: The opening small talk and 15th-anniversary congratulations, about 1 minute, can be skipped.

points.h: The old cross-border mega-seller playbook is dead
points.body: Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-style mindset, running dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths, and plenty of investors loved them. But a distribution-style company is essentially a traffic-style company: the more stores, the more likely you are to get traffic. When a platform's goods aren't plentiful enough, he doesn't oppose distribution; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, there are three red lines: goods not matching the listing harms consumers, brushing orders harms other merchants, and slipping in little cards to build private traffic harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel cares deeply about consumer experience, and these behaviours run straight into that protective wall.

points.h: Of the four choices, region comes first
points.body: Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce — all of life is about choice mattering more than effort. He gives four choices: region, channel, product category, brand positioning. On region he has always argued for seizing the European and US markets first, because paying power is strong, internet penetration is high, and more importantly a brand can build momentum there. This isn't something they invented: when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized Europe and the US. On category, they change their advice every three years: the first three years they backed products common to China and abroad, where the domestic supply chain could sell overseas without modification — like Anker's power banks, which back then were almost identical apart from the voltage; the second three years they advised overseas-exclusive products, because China's supply chain had all gone overseas and China-abroad commonality offered no differentiation; the last three years it's product 3.0 — powered, chipped, algorithmic.

points.h: It's not that you go to Europe and the US once you're big — you go there to get big
points.body: Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to Europe and the US when I'm big’; he says it's exactly backwards — you go to Europe and the US so you can get big. He cites the swimwear company Cupshe: a husband and wife, 50,000 dollars of inventory, and the first stop was the US. 50,000 dollars is sales inventory, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. Looking recently at AI smart hardware, they start from a thousand or ten thousand products on the Kickstarter crowdfunding platform, even taking prepayment before placing orders, with no capital — that's also a great way to test the water. He even advises big companies entering the European and US markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce through; big and small companies alike should first nail the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

points.h: After AI, good companies don't just find demand — they create it
points.body: Wei Zhe says that with AI, excellent companies shouldn't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He cites a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally unpowered, they electrified it, added a chip and an algorithm — the algorithm is actually very simple, with GPS positioning, since the map of the sky's movements is regular. He wasn't an astronomy hobbyist before but would buy one: at home in Silicon Valley you tap once, it automatically aligns Orion for you, tells you three in the morning is the best time, you set it and go to sleep, and the next day it has taken the shots for you. This lets anyone become a very good astronomy hobbyist. Another example: a cross-border class student doing curtains, which didn't sell well in the US after being powered, because American electricians are expensive; so he put a solar panel on the window, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into something you can DIY. Revenue went from one or two hundred million to four or five hundred million, and profit is now one or two hundred million.

points.h: In the AI era, still charging subscriptions means you're behind
points.body: Wei Zhe says that in the AI era, still thinking in terms of subscription fees means you're behind again; they're all urging companies toward back-end charging, software charging — tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest approach, a bit like advertising that used to charge by time rather than by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for the month a waste of two weeks? They advise that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not go back to the old SaaS model of 9.99 dollars a month. One AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and charges nothing if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers — after topping up, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

points.h: Adding AI is more worth backing than AI adding
points.body: Wei Zhe has a view he calls AI-plus versus plus-AI; he flips the phrase around and says he's more bullish on plus-AI than on today's AI-plus. The difference: plus-AI is hardware humans have already accepted, which you AI-ify; rather than using AI to create hardware never seen before. It's very hard for humans to accept an entirely new piece of hardware. Take Oura making a ring, because you accepted rings first; something that hangs a camera under your neck is harder for me — I've never accepted that hardware. So they're very bullish on adding AI to already-accepted hardware. One capacitive stylus they invested in is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad; it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies that pen. He also particularly wants to transform one of the top one or two overseas fitness-equipment companies, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with an AI-generated one — you want a man, it's a man; you want a Black coach, it's a Black coach; install two cameras and it can coach your workout with AI.

points.h: Channels aren't laid out flat — they're a pyramid
points.body: Wei Zhe says channels aren't about more channels meaning more roads, with each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and rules about which channel a new product launches in first. What counts as a light-goods channel, what counts as the main waist channel for volume — the pyramid design differs by category and brand. He cites Anker: making power banks and mecha gear seems a bit low, so to enter the consumer-electronics high ground of Soundcore headphones it had to get into Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot doesn't matter, but it can transform the brand — Apple is the pinnacle of the pyramid. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street; even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose — but it must hold that position. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work: AliExpress is a light-goods channel, somewhere to dump stock after Amazon delists you; you can't sell on Amazon and here too, and consumers get confused.

points.h: R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0
points.body: Wei Zhe says he really dislikes splashing out on marketing spend. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are happy to add 2% of revenue to marketing spend, but consumers don't get it. He says: do you dare add 2% of revenue to R&D spend? He has met many bosses at the one or two billion scale; at one billion they say 20 million for R&D, and I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem — you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing spend makes the platform happy and consumers get nothing; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed a good product speaks for itself, and marketing is just — your R&D is the 1, marketing is the 0; if your thing is good you can amplify it, but if you don't have that 1, absolutely don't put on a lot of 0s. He gives three signals for judging: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and crush it by doubling its performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online and hit a point where offline channels come looking for you.

points.h: AI doesn't just change products — it rebuilds every role
points.body: Wei Zhe says AI matters to companies in two ways, and big, medium and small companies all need to do both well: first, combining products with AI; second, how the organisation changes through AI. He sees cross-border e-commerce companies as, of almost all industries he has seen, the ones that most should use AI to transform every role. Every role should ask what AI can do for you: product selection, content generation, ad placement choices — all essentially algorithms; previously it relied on human experience, and experience is definitely not as strong as algorithmic iteration. Customer service AI-ified: there is no customer service anymore, customer service is just you training your customer-service agent; for ad placement you train an agent; product selection, product display, product image and video generation all AI-ified. He says this is the first and only industry he has seen where the entire company's organisational chain can all be transformed by AI. He also says what they oppose most is putting lots of people overseas — with or without AI they oppose it; it's called: no unnecessary people placed overseas.

points.h: Don't just let AI do the work — let it into the decisions
points.body: Wei Zhe puts AI and organisation very simply: many companies have a P series and an M series — P is the professional series, M is management. Many people are used to letting AI do P work, doing the job; generating images was originally P-series work. But truly formidable companies don't just let AI do P-series work; they gradually let it do the work a Manager, Director or VP should do. He gives a real AI pricing case: the company originally wanted to sell at 35 euros, AI said you can sell at 55, the company really went to 55 and it really sold, volume about the same as at 35 before, but 20 euros more profit. He says AI has no courage, but it's bolder than you — it has compared everything across the whole web for you. He also says that even if AI hallucinates, with so many large models across China and the US, they won't all dream the same dream at the same time, so you must cross-validate.
